title: Whisky and Chocolate Pairing | Craft Beer School
desc: Whisky and chocolate pairing: shared flavours from oak and roasting, which cocoa percentage suits which cask and how to taste a flight in Indian heat.
teaser: Oak and roasted cacao share a surprising number of flavours. Here is how to make them meet in the glass.
standfirst: Chocolate is one of the easiest foods to pair with whisky, because the two share flavours from roasting, toasting and fermentation. Get the sweetness right and the match is excellent. Get it wrong and the whisky tastes hot and thin.
sections: Chocolate and whisky share flavours from similar processes

Cacao beans are fermented, dried and roasted before they become chocolate. Whisky starts as a fermented grain wash and picks up much of its flavour from casks that were toasted or charred. Heat and fermentation create overlapping families of flavour in both: caramel, roasted nuts, dried fruit, coffee and vanilla.

Vanilla is the clearest link. Oak contains lignin, which breaks down during toasting into vanillin, the main flavour compound in vanilla. That is why bourbon, matured in new charred oak, so often smells of vanilla. Milk chocolate is often flavoured with vanilla too. The two meet halfway.
Match the cocoa to the cask

• Milk chocolate (around 30 to 40% cocoa) with bourbon or a bourbon cask malt. Vanilla meets vanilla, caramel meets caramel.
  • Dark chocolate around 70% with a sherry cask malt. Dried fruit and spice against bitter cocoa.
  • Very dark chocolate, 85% or more, with a peated or cask strength whisky. Both are intense enough to hold their ground.
  • Orange or salted dark chocolate with a lighter Speyside or Irish whiskey. The extra flavour bridges to fruit.

White chocolate is mostly cocoa butter, sugar and milk. It is very sweet and suits only the sweetest, softest whiskies.

Sweet food makes a drink taste less sweet, more bitter and more alcoholic. Chocolate is sweet, so it pulls the sweetness out of whatever whisky you drink after it. A dry, oaky whisky can suddenly taste harsh.

The fix is to choose sweeter, richer whiskies for sweeter chocolates and save the drier, smokier ones for very dark chocolate with little sugar. If a pairing tastes hot and thin, the chocolate is too sweet for that whisky.

Strength matters as well. A cask strength whisky at 55% or more can numb the palate before the chocolate has a chance. Add a few drops of water to it first, taste again, then bring in the chocolate.

The order matters. Taste the whisky first, on its own, so you know its baseline. Then put a small square of chocolate on your tongue and let it melt rather than chewing it. Cocoa butter melts at about 34 °C, just below body temperature, so it coats the mouth slowly as it warms.

When the chocolate has half melted, take a small sip of whisky. The alcohol mixes with the fat and sugar and new flavours often appear. Then sip once more after the chocolate has gone. Note what changed each time.

Chocolate is best stored somewhere cool and dry, below about 20 °C. In much of India that means the fridge. Take it out 10 to 15 minutes before tasting so it is not rock hard. Keep it wrapped while it warms so condensation does not form. Moisture on the surface dissolves sugar that later dries as a white, dusty bloom.

India grows cacao, mainly in Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. A number of Indian bean-to-bar makers now produce single-origin dark chocolates. Tasting one alongside an Indian single malt makes a satisfying all-Indian flight; see our guide to Indian single malt.

Choose three whiskies and three chocolates. Cut the chocolate into small squares of about 5 g. Pour 15 ml of each whisky. Put water and plain crackers on the table to reset the palate between rounds.

Work through each whisky with each chocolate, lightest first. You will taste nine combinations without drinking much. Keep notes as you go; by the third whisky the earlier pairs blur. A sheet of paper under the glasses with each name written on it stops anyone losing track of which pour is which. Our guide to whisky and cheese uses the same method if you want to try another flight.

The most common mistake is serving too much of both. Big pours and big pieces overload the palate until everything starts tasting the same. The second is pairing very sweet chocolate with a dry whisky, which makes the spirit taste harsh. The third is cold chocolate straight from the fridge, which barely melts and tastes of little.

All three are easy to fix. Smaller portions, the right sweetness and a few minutes of warming do most of the work.
Start with one bar and two whiskies

Buy a single 70% dark chocolate. Pour 15 ml each of two contrasting whiskies, perhaps a bourbon and a sherry cask malt. Taste each whisky alone, then with the chocolate. Write down which pair you preferred and why.

That one comparison tells you whether your palate leans toward echo pairings or contrast pairings. Build your next flight around the answer.
faqs: Dark chocolate around 70% cocoa is the most versatile. Milk chocolate suits bourbon; very dark chocolate suits peated or strong whiskies.
Should I eat the chocolate before or after the whisky?
Taste the whisky first, then let a square of chocolate half melt on your tongue before sipping again.
Why does whisky taste harsh with chocolate?
Sweet chocolate makes whisky taste less sweet and more alcoholic. Try a darker chocolate or a sweeter whisky.
